0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter shows the rougher, more Semitic Greek one would expect from a Galilean fisherman writing more directly. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels, Noah, Sodom; the Balaam archetype; the waterless springs; the dog and pig proverbs). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire. For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love. For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins. Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
1.overview:
The opening chapter lays the theological foundation for everything that follows. God's divine power has already given believers everything needed for life and godliness (v. 3) — the indicative is total and complete. From that foundation the imperative rises: make every effort, add to your faith, be diligent (vv. 5, 10). The letter opens with lavish gift and closes the chapter with urgent command — not as contradiction but as the grammar of grace. What God has fully provided, the believer is to fully pursue.

The second half of the chapter (vv. 12–21) grounds Peter's authority in two things: the apostolic eyewitness of the Transfiguration and the prophetic Scriptures. These are not two competing sources but two interlocking confirmations — history and prophecy, the visible and the written, pointing to the same Christ and the same coming Day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The opening four verses are a compressed systematic theology: God's divine power has given us everything (v. 3); through his precious and very great promises we share in the divine nature itself (v. 4). This is the most striking claim Peter ever makes — not that God gives us gifts alongside himself, but that he gives himself, his own moral nature, as the gift. The virtue chain of vv. 5–7 flows from that gift: because we have been made partakers of the divine nature, we are to build on faith the very qualities that characterize that nature.

The chain is a literary device called a sorites — also called a climax in rhetoric — in which each quality becomes the base for the next, so that the structure itself embodies the argument — virtue builds on virtue, each resting on the one before. The same device appears in Romans 5:3–5 (suffering → endurance → character → hope) and James 1:3–4. The goal is a fully furnished Christian — neither idle nor unfruitful (v. 8), neither nearsighted nor amnesiac (v. 9), neither unstable nor excluded (vv. 10–11).

The theology and the exhortation together answer the false teachers of ch. 2, who promise freedom while demonstrating none of these virtues. The authentic community looks entirely different from the counterfeit one.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4) — this phrase has generated more theological controversy than almost any other in the letter. Three misreadings must be ruled out first: (1) It is not the Orthodox idea of becoming God or merging into the divine essence — Peter immediately defines it as escaping the corruption of the world through sinful desire, which is moral and relational, not ontological. (2) It is not pantheism — the phrase describes participation, not identity. (3) It is not merely metaphorical — Peter uses the most striking language available to convey that what is transferred is genuinely God's own character. The Reformed understanding: believers participate in God's moral attributes — his holiness, love, patience, truth — not in his incommunicable attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, aseity). Calvin: we are so united to Christ that we share in what belongs to him. The new birth (1 Pet 1:23) is the mechanism; the divine nature is the content; moral transformation is the evidence.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation member asks: 'Am I really expected to have all seven of those virtues? I can barely manage patience.' The sorites chain answers: start with faith. Faith is given. From faith, press toward moral excellence. The chain does not demand that all seven appear simultaneously and fully formed — it demands that the direction is right and the effort is real. The person with genuine faith will be reaching for virtue; the person with genuine virtue will hunger for knowledge; and so on. The chain is a trajectory before it is a checklist. The person who has stopped reaching — who is comfortable with faith alone and sees no need to press further — is the nearsighted, closed-eyed person Peter describes: having forgotten his cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Simeon Peter' (v. 1) — the double name is distinctive. 'Simeon' is the Hebrew/Aramaic form (used at the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15:14); 'Peter' is the Greek rendering of the Aramaic 'Kēpha' — the Rock — that Jesus gave him. The combination reads like a man announcing both his origins and his calling: the Galilean fisherman and the Rock of the church. Pseudepigraphers do not typically make their self-identification this ethnically precise.

'Equal standing' (v. 1) — the word carries the sense of equal value, equal honor: like coins of equal worth, like citizens with equal rights in a new colony. Peter's recipients — scattered, socially marginal, facing the same false teachers as the apostles — have received the exact same currency of faith as the Twelve. There are no premium and economy grades of Christian faith.

'Our God and Savior Jesus Christ' — a single article governs both nouns, invoking Granville Sharp's Rule: when a single article governs two nouns joined by 'and,' they refer to the same person. Peter calls Jesus 'our God and Savior' — a direct affirmation of Christ's full deity at the letter's opening. The same construction appears in Titus 2:13.

The divine power (v. 3) has already acted: everything needed for life and godliness is already given, already transferred, already operative. The believer is not waiting for a second endowment. Through full, transforming knowledge — not the Gnostics' claim to elite secret knowledge, but the real, relational, life-altering knowing of God that Peter returns to in 1:2, 3, 8 — all of it has already come to every believer.

'Partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4) — the boldest phrase in the letter. The mechanism: God's precious and very great promises are the vehicle through which the divine nature is communicated. The promises of the gospel, believed and received, transfer God's own moral character into the believer. The contrast is with corruption and decay — the word describes both moral rot and the physical dissolution of the fallen world. The divine nature and worldly corruption are mutually exclusive; to participate in one is to escape the other.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seven-virtue chain (vv. 5–7) is a rhetorical climax — each quality becomes the base for the next, so that the structure itself embodies the argument: virtue builds on virtue. The chain: faith → moral excellence (the same word used of God himself in v. 3, where it describes his own glory — to cultivate this excellence is to pattern oneself after the God who called you) → practical wisdom for living → self-control, the mastery of the appetites → steadfastness, the capacity to hold under pressure without breaking → godliness, a reverent orientation toward God in all of life → brotherly affection, love for the community of faith → and finally love, the self-giving love that extends beyond the community to the world.

'Make every effort' (v. 5) conveys urgency and diligence. The Christian life is not passive. The divine power has given everything; the believer is to pursue everything. Grace and effort are not competitors — grace is the ground, effort is the response.

The person without these virtues is spiritually nearsighted (v. 9) — literally 'closing the eyes to see only what is near,' preoccupied with immediate comfort, unable to see the kingdom's horizon. The linked diagnosis is 'having forgotten' — the word is the same as the mythological river Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld, and the root of our word 'lethal.' The person who lacks the virtues has forgotten his cleansing — the definitive break of baptism and new birth is no longer the operative fact of his self-understanding.

The entrance into the eternal kingdom will be richly provided (v. 11). The same verb used for what the believer supplies to his faith in v. 5 now describes what God supplies at the end — a beautiful divine reciprocity that is not merit but grace responding to faith's fruitfulness.

Verse 10 — 'Make your calling and election sure': This is the verse every Arminian reaches for, and every Reformed preacher must be ready to explain. Does it mean that election is conditional on virtue — that you secure your election by adding these qualities? No — and the grammar confirms it. The verb is middle voice: make sure for yourselves, not make sure before God. The purpose is assurance, not merit. Peter is not saying 'accumulate enough virtue and God will elect you'; he is saying 'the fruit you produce will confirm to your own conscience, and to watching eyes around you, that your calling and election are real.' Election is God's unilateral, unconditional decree (Eph. 1:4); assurance of election is partly the fruit of the Spirit's work in producing these very qualities. Calvin: 'He does not say that they are to obtain election by their works, but that they are to make it sure and certain to themselves.' The person who lacks these qualities (v. 9) does not thereby lose their election — but they lose their assurance of it, and they give watching unbelievers no reason to believe the gospel is real. The stakes of sanctification are therefore both personal and evangelistic.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Why should the recipients trust Peter's teaching? He gives two answers in this section, and together they form the epistemological foundation of Christian confidence: the apostolic eyewitness (vv. 16–18) and the prophetic Scripture (vv. 19–21). These are not competing sources — they are two interlocking confirmations. The Transfiguration was the visible, historical event in which the Father announced the Son's glory; the prophetic Scriptures are the textual witness that anticipated and now illuminates that event. History confirms prophecy; prophecy interprets history.

Peter writes near death. The urgency is existential: he is making arrangements for the community to have access to his teaching after he is gone (v. 15). What follows in the letter — the portrait of the false teachers, the eschatological certainties of ch. 3 — is his final pastoral investment. The man who three times denied Christ and was three times restored is now spending his last days ensuring the church can stand without him.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 20–21 are the NT's most explicit statement of the divine origin of Scripture: 'no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.' The word 'carried along' is the same word used in v. 17 for the voice 'borne' to Peter on the holy mountain — a deliberate verbal link binding the Transfiguration and the prophetic word under the same divine motive power. Just as the voice was carried to Peter by God's own initiative, so the prophets were carried by the Spirit — their personalities, vocabularies, and circumstances were all used, but the motive force was divine. The sailing metaphor is exact: the sailors do not make the wind, but they set the sails, and the wind drives the ship where it wills. This is the Reformed doctrine of concursive inspiration: fully human, fully divine.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation member who grew up with the Bible asks: 'Why should I trust the OT prophets — they wrote so long ago, in such different circumstances?' Peter's answer: the prophetic word is like a lamp in a dark, gloomy, airless room. When you are in that room, you do not argue with the lamp. You read by it. The dark place is the present age; the lamp is the Scripture that illuminates it. You hold the lamp until the day fully dawns — until Christ returns and the full light of the kingdom makes lamps unnecessary. Until then, the lamp is not optional.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This body' (v. 13) — the word Peter uses is 'tent/tabernacle,' the same family as the word behind 'the Word tabernacled among us' in John 1:14. The portability and temporariness of the tent conveys imminent departure. Peter is aware he is in the last season of his earthly life, and the image captures both the fragility and the dignity of embodied existence: a tent is temporary, but it shelters real life.

'The putting off of my body will be soon' — 'putting off' like removing a garment. Peter is not afraid of death; it is something to be taken off and set aside. The Lord Jesus had told him this would come — a reference to John 21:18–19, where Jesus predicted that Peter would be led where he did not wish to go, signifying what death he would die. Tradition records Peter's crucifixion in Rome under Nero, upside down at his own request (Origen; Eusebius). He writes knowing the appointment.

'Departure' (v. 15) — the word Peter uses for his own death is the same word used at the Transfiguration, when Moses and Elijah 'spoke of his departure which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem' (Luke 9:31, ESV margin: 'exodus'). Peter uses the same word for his own death. His death is, like Christ's, an exodus — not an ending but a passing through, a going-out toward something greater. The man who was present on the holy mountain heard this word applied to Christ; now he applies the same word to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,' we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Cleverly devised myths' (v. 16) — the false teachers were almost certainly calling the apostolic proclamation of Christ's return a 'myth,' a cleverly constructed story. Peter turns the accusation: we did not follow myths; we followed what we saw. The very sophistication implied in 'cleverly' is the accusation turned back on itself — sophisticated fabrication is precisely what Peter did not practice.

'Eyewitnesses' (v. 16) — the word is borrowed from the Eleusinian mystery religions, where it described the highest grade of initiate, the one admitted to see the final secret. The mysteries promised their initiates an intimate vision of the divine through theatrical revelation. Peter uses this language and claims something far beyond it: we were eyewitnesses — not of a staged theatrical revelation, but of the uncreated glory of God overshadowing the Son of Man on a holy mountain.

'The Majestic Glory' (v. 17) — a phrase found nowhere else in the NT, reserved for the divine shekinah presence on the mountain. Tradition names it as Tabor (in Galilee) or, more likely given the geographical context of Matthew 16–17, Mount Hermon in the north.

The Transfiguration is Peter's supreme credential. He does not argue for the parousia from deduction or from tradition passed down from others; he was there when the Father announced the Son's glory on the holy mountain. Significantly, the word used for the voice 'borne' to him on the mountain is the same word that appears in v. 21 for the Spirit carrying the prophets along. Divine speech — whether at the Transfiguration or through the prophets — is always borne to its recipients by God's own initiative.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts, knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The prophetic word made more sure' (v. 19) — two readings are possible: (a) the prophetic word has been further confirmed by the Transfiguration; the eyewitness event validates what the OT already said; (b) the prophetic word is more sure than even eyewitness experience, because written Scripture is inherently more certain than human memory and testimony. The ESV margin captures both. Either way, the prophetic Scriptures and the apostolic eyewitness point to the same reality and reinforce each other.

'A lamp shining in a dark place' (v. 19) — the word for 'dark' means dusty, squalid, gloomy — not just dark but airless and oppressive. The present age, without Scripture, is that kind of place. The OT prophetic word is the lamp that makes the age navigable. The lamp serves until the day fully dawns — until the parousia brings full light and lamps become unnecessary. Until then, the lamp is not supplementary; it is essential.

'The morning star' (v. 19) — the planet Venus, which appears just before dawn and announces the coming day. In Isaiah 14:12 the Babylonian king is satirized as 'day star, son of the dawn.' In Revelation 22:16 Jesus claims the title 'the bright morning star.' The morning star rises 'in your hearts' — the dawning of the full Day of the Lord is not merely an external cosmic event but an inward transformation. The expectation and the reality meet within the believer.

'No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation' (v. 20) — this phrase has been contested for centuries. Three options: (1) Roman Catholic reading: no individual reader can interpret Scripture independently — the Magisterium alone determines meaning. But this reads far too much into the text, which says nothing about readers at all. (2) Majority Reformed reading (Grudem, ESV): the prophecy did not arise from the prophet's own interpretation of events — the prophet did not sit down and interpret the situation and produce his own message. The grammar supports this: 'interpretation' means the prophet's own explanatory origination of the message. (3) A third option: prophecy does not have a private/personal origin at all. All three readings converge on the same point confirmed by v. 21: 'no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.' The word for 'carried along' is the same word used in v. 17 for the voice borne to Peter on the mountain. The prophets were the instruments; the Spirit was the wind. Their personalities, vocabularies, and circumstances were genuinely employed — but they did not originate the message. This is concursive inspiration: fully human, fully divine, without confusion or competition.

1.theology:
The chapter's great theological claim is 'partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4). This is not deification in the Orthodox sense (we do not become God or merge into the divine essence) nor pantheism (we do not become part of God). It is moral participation: through the Spirit and through union with Christ, God's own character — his holiness, patience, love, truthfulness — is communicated to the believer. Calvin: we are so united to Christ that we share in what belongs to him. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification is nothing less than the outworking of this participation: the divine nature expressing itself in human virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is not a human document about God; it is God's own word spoken through human instruments. The Spirit carried the prophets; therefore the prophets' words carry divine authority. This is why Peter can describe the prophetic word as 'more sure' than even his own eyewitness — the written word outlasts the eyewitness, is available to all, and carries the authority not of human testimony but of the Spirit who inspired it.
1.examples:
The virtue chain (vv. 5–7) addresses a perennial pastoral problem: Christians who park at faith and see no need to move. 'I believe — isn't that enough?' Peter's answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. A Christian who has been given the divine nature and is not building virtue, knowledge, and love is like a person given a magnificent musical instrument who never practices. The gift is real; the neglect is also real; and the result is the same — no music. The preacher should note that Peter does not make the virtues the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence of its reality and the trajectory of its growth.

The lamp-and-morning-star image (v. 19) is a pastoral gift for believers who feel that Scripture reading is dry and unproductive. You do not read the Bible because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the only lamp available. The darkness is not a reason to put the lamp down. The lamp is precisely what a dark place requires.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep. For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly; and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked — then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter's sustained portrait of the false teacher — his methods (secret infiltration), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motivation (greed), and his destiny (condemnation already certain). Peter establishes the certainty of judgment through three historical examples — fallen angels, Noah's generation, Sodom and Gomorrah — and then turns to a detailed characterization of the teachers themselves: arrogant, irrational, greedy, enslaved to the very passions they indulge.

The chapter's controlling irony is in vv. 19: they promise freedom while being themselves slaves of corruption. The false teacher is always selling something he does not possess. The authentic test of any teacher is not the sophistication of his language but the shape of his life — and the false teacher's life betrays him at every point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10a — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter opens with a historical parallel that frames everything: as Israel had false prophets who corrupted the covenant community from within, so the church will have false teachers who corrupt it from within. The parallel is not accidental — it signals that internal corruption is the characteristic danger of the covenant people in every age. The Baal prophets did not come from outside Israel; they arose within it. So too these teachers.

The three examples (angels, Noah, Sodom) function as a legal brief: God has an established pattern of judging the wicked and delivering the righteous. The false teachers are not facing something unprecedented; they are walking into a pattern God has already demonstrated three times. Lot's rescue is the chapter's pastoral surprise — a righteous man whose compromised circumstances did not nullify his genuine righteousness or his distress at the wickedness around him.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Denying the Master who bought them' (v. 1). The word for 'Master' is the strongest available — absolute master, sovereign, not the gentler 'Lord.' And he 'bought them' — redemption language (1 Cor 6:20; Rev 5:9). Two Reformed positions on whether this implies genuine prior salvation: (a) the language of covenant membership — these teachers belong to the visible church and have received the external benefits of the covenant (as in 1 Cor 10, where those who ate the manna and crossed the sea nonetheless fell in the wilderness); (b) 'bought' refers to creation and general preservation as image-bearers, not to saving redemption. Either way, the desertion is high-handed and without excuse: they have denied the very One who gave them everything they have.
verseByVerse.examples: Lot's rescue (vv. 7–8) is a pastoral gift. Peter calls Lot 'righteous' three times (vv. 7, 8) — a striking description of a man who chose to live in Sodom, who delayed when angels told him to flee, and who offered his daughters to the mob. Yet his soul was 'tormented day after day' by what he saw. Peter is not endorsing Lot's choices; he is insisting that genuine righteousness can coexist with compromised circumstances and even grievous errors. The person who lives in a corrupt environment, feels its corruption as agony rather than pleasure, and would leave if they could — that person is Lot. God knows how to rescue them.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
False prophets arose among Israel; false teachers will arise among the church. The OT/NT parallel is deliberate. The covenant community has never been immune to internal corruption. This is not pessimism but realism grounded in the OT's own testimony.

'Will secretly bring in alongside' (v. 1) — the very word conveys the method: they do not announce themselves as heterodox; they enter alongside the truth, like weeds among wheat. The same word appears in Jude 4 ('crept in'). The method of the false teacher is never frontal assault but gradual infiltration.

'Destructive heresies' (v. 1) — 'heresy' began as a word for a choosing, then a school of thought, then a faction. Here it means factions or teachings that lead to destruction, the opposite of salvation. The teachers bring their followers toward the very destination they claim to help them escape.

'Will exploit you' (v. 3) — the word is a commercial term: to travel as a merchant, to trade for profit. The same root gives us 'emporium.' The false teacher's relationship to his congregation is transactional: they are merchandise, a revenue stream. The manufactured words — 'molded' or 'fabricated' words, the root of our word 'plastic' — are the product he sells.

'The Master who bought them' (v. 1): This phrase has generated significant debate. Does Peter teach that Christ died for people who ultimately perish — falsifying particular redemption? Three observations. First, the word 'Master' emphasises absolute ownership and lordship; the purchase language may refer to God's covenant ownership of Israel (Deut. 32:6; Isa. 63:16) rather than Christ's atoning death specifically. Second, even if atoning purchase is in view, the false teachers are being described in their own self-presentation within the covenant community — they claimed to belong to the Master; Peter turns their own claim against them. Third, the Reformed tradition (Owen, Murray, Packer) has consistently argued that 'buying' in covenantal contexts describes a relationship of ownership and obligation, not necessarily an efficacious redemptive act for each individual. The main point stands regardless of how the atonement question is resolved: these teachers have repudiated the very Lord who has every claim over them — by creation, by covenant, by the community they joined — and the guilt of that repudiation is correspondingly severe.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly; and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked — then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three examples are structured as a single long conditional sentence (if... if... if... then): if God acted in judgment and deliverance in each of these three cases, then he both can and will do so again. The argument is from precedent.

Example 1 — the angels (v. 4). The word for 'cast them into hell' — used only here in the NT — is literally 'tartarized.' Tartaros was in Greek mythology the deepest pit, below Hades, where the Titans were imprisoned. Peter uses this term, familiar to his Hellenistic readers, to describe the place of confinement for the angels who sinned. The background is almost certainly Genesis 6:1–4 (the 'sons of God' who took human wives) as interpreted in 1 Enoch 6–16, a text widely known in first-century Judaism. Peter does not endorse 1 Enoch as Scripture; he uses the tradition as a shared cultural reference point, just as Paul quotes Aratus in Acts 17. A textual variant reads 'pits of gloomy darkness' instead of 'chains'; both yield the same image of secure confinement in darkness.

Example 2 — Noah (v. 5). 'Eighth' — Noah was the eighth person preserved (he and seven family members). 'Herald of righteousness' — Noah is not just a survivor; he is a preacher. The same God who judged the world preserved a witness to his righteousness. Judgment and proclamation coexist.

Example 3 — Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 6–7). The word for 'turning to ashes' is the origin of the English 'catastrophe.' The cities become a public display of what judgment looks like for those who live in godlessness. Lot is called righteous — three times in vv. 7–8. His soul was tormented day after day by what he saw and heard. The word used is the strongest available for anguish — the language of testing metals on a touchstone or of torture on the rack. Genuine righteousness feels the wickedness of its environment as torment, not as entertainment.

The conclusion (vv. 9–10a): the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial. The same divine knowledge that executes judgment also executes rescue. The false teacher's congregants need not fear that God has lost track of them in the midst of the corruption they inhabit.

Why is Lot called ‘righteous’? (vv. 7–8): This is the question every congregation asks. Lot in Genesis is not an obviously impressive figure: he chose Sodom, lingered when angels urged him to flee, offered his daughters to the mob, and ended in a cave in incest. Why does Peter call him righteous — three times in two verses? The answer is the doctrine of justification. Lot was righteous by faith in God’s covenant promises, not by the quality of his conduct — the same imputed righteousness credited to Abraham (Gen. 15:6), the same forensic standing every sinner receives through union with Christ. Peter’s point is not that Lot was morally exemplary but that he was a genuine believer whose soul was daily tormented by the lawless conduct around him. Two pastoral applications: First, genuine faith does not guarantee a life of obvious moral strength — Lot is a sobering warning against measuring the reality of faith by its outward impressiveness. Second, the righteous person living among the wicked pays a real price — the daily grinding of a redeemed conscience in an unredeemed environment. God saw it in Lot’s case. He sees it now. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly (v. 9) — and He counts the cost they have paid.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10b–22 — The Portrait of the False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established the certainty of judgment through three historical examples, Peter now turns to a sustained portrait of the false teachers themselves. He works through their arrogance toward heavenly powers (vv. 10b–11), their irrationality (v. 12), their greed (vv. 13–16, climaxing in the Balaam archetype), and their ultimate futility (vv. 17–22).

The Balaam section (vv. 14–16) is the chapter's interpretive key. Balaam was the OT's supreme example of the prophet who hired out his gift for money — a man with genuine prophetic access to God who sold that access to the highest bidder. He is the patron saint of religious professionalism corrupted by greed. The false teachers are his heirs.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 20–22 raise one of the most pastorally urgent questions in the letter: can someone who has genuinely escaped the world's corruption through the knowledge of the Lord Jesus fall back into it and be worse off than before? Peter says plainly: yes. The Reformed response is not to deny this but to distinguish: the knowledge these people had may have been external and covenantal — real participation in the visible community, real exposure to the gospel's transforming power — without the inward regeneration that produces perseverance. The parallel is 1 Corinthians 10: the Israelites who ate the manna and crossed the sea and 'were all baptized into Moses' nonetheless fell in the wilderness. The dog and the pig are not changed in their nature by the bath or the meal; they return to what they fundamentally are. This does not threaten the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints; it defines the boundary of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The waterless springs image (v. 17) is a precise pastoral diagnosis. In a Palestinian summer, the sight of a spring is the sight of life. A traveler crosses the hills toward a spring and finds it dry. The false teacher creates exactly this experience: he generates the expectation of life-giving refreshment, and the congregation arrives thirsty and finds nothing. The preacher should ask: do my people leave refreshed — fed from the Word, met by Christ, equipped for the week — or have they come to a spring and found dust?

verseByVerse.quote: Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord. These, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Bold and self-willed' (v. 10b) — self-will as the defining characteristic: the false teacher is one who pleases himself above all else, bold not in righteousness but in self-assertion. Contrast the angels (v. 11) who, though 'greater in might and power,' do not speak rashly against even the fallen angelic powers — they leave judgment to the Lord. The false teachers have less caution than archangels.

'Irrational animals, creatures of instinct' (v. 12) — the word means literally 'without reason, without the ordering principle that structures rational existence.' The same Logos that undergirds creation and revelation is the principle these teachers have abandoned. They function like animals: driven by appetite, born only to be consumed by the very desires they serve.

'Balaam of Bosor' (v. 15) — in Numbers 22–24, Balaam is called son of Beor; 'Bosor' is likely a dialect form. Balaam was a genuine prophet — God did speak through him — who repeatedly attempted to curse Israel for financial reward from Balak, king of Moab. When direct curses failed, he advised Balak to use Moabite women to seduce Israel into idolatry (Num 31:16). He is the archetypal figure of religious gift deployed in service of personal gain. 'He loved the wages of unrighteousness' (v. 15) — he loved the money. The same phrase appears in Acts 1:18 of Judas. Peter links the two men: the prophet who sold his gift and the apostle who sold his Lord share the same love.

The donkey's rebuke (v. 16): Balaam's madness — derangement, being beside one's mind — was checked by a mute animal speaking in a human voice. A prophet who was also a professional communicator was corrected by a beast of burden. The irony is maximal and intentional: when a man's greed takes him beyond the bounds of reason, even a donkey has more sense than he does.

'Blaspheme the glorious ones' (vv. 10b–11): 'The glorious ones' are almost certainly angelic beings — a term for the celestial powers and authorities that govern the created order. The false teachers were speaking contemptuously of angelic powers, probably as part of their libertine theology: if the angelic authorities that administer moral boundaries are dismissible, then the moral law they enforce can be ignored. Peter's counter is devastating: even the greatest angels — greater in might and power than these teachers — do not bring a slanderous judgment against the glorious ones before the Lord. Jude 9 gives the specific example: Michael, the archangel, disputing with the devil over Moses's body, said not 'I condemn you' but 'The Lord rebuke you.' The lesser beings (the false teachers) blaspheme those who are greater — something the greatest angels refuse to do toward the fallen. The preacher's application: contempt for divine order, spiritual authority, or the structures God has placed in creation is not spiritual sophistication. It is an arrogance that surpasses even the fallen angels in its audacity.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A spring without water is worse than no spring at all: it creates expectation and then destroys it. In Palestinian geography, a reliable spring was the difference between life and death for a community. The false teacher creates the appearance of the life-giving water of the Word while delivering nothing. He is like mist driven by a storm: all movement and noise, no substance or nourishment. The contrast with ch. 1's virtue chain is complete: genuine growth is slow, solid, and cumulative; the false teacher is dramatic, shifting, and empty.

'Great swelling words' (v. 18) — inflated, bloated rhetoric, maximally impressive and minimally substantive. The false teacher's rhetoric is maximally impressive and minimally substantive. He promises freedom while being himself a slave — 'whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved' (v. 19). Slavery is the fate of the conquered. The man who promises freedom has been conquered by his own appetites.

The dog and pig proverbs (vv. 21–22). The dog returns to its own vomit (Prov 26:11, the only OT proverb cited as such in 2 Peter) and the sow, after washing, returns to roll in the mire. Both animals are unclean in Jewish law; the combination doubles the force. The key detail: the sow has been washed — a full, complete cleansing. And returns to the mud. The nature of the animal is unchanged by the external cleansing. This does not mean that all apostates were never genuinely converted — it means that external cleansing without internal transformation produces this result. The preacher must hold this honestly: the visible church contains both the truly born again and those who have been washed externally but whose nature is unchanged.

2.theology: The chapter's controlling theological question is the nature of apostasy. Can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer: those truly regenerate will persevere (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). But the visible church contains those who participate in covenant privileges without possessing covenant life — and it is these who can experience the knowledge described in v. 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and pig proverbs define the boundary: the animal's nature is unchanged. External reformation without regeneration leads to greater corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the doctrine's honest context.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives the congregation diagnostic tools. The false teacher's test is not doctrinal sophistication but financial transparency: What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear (and therefore what they will pay to hear)? Balaam was a genuine prophet whose gift was real — but the gift became a commodity. The test of authentic ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The final chapter is the letter's destination. Everything in chapters 1 and 2 has been preparation for this: the false teachers are dangerous not merely because they are immoral but because they have attacked the hope — the promise of Christ's return — and by doing so have severed the ethical nerve of the Christian life. If the Day is not coming, why be holy? If the Lord will not appear, why resist the flesh? The scoffers have grasped this logic and pressed it into service of their own licentiousness.

Peter's response is one of the most carefully constructed arguments in the New Testament. He does not simply reassert the promise; he dismantles the philosophical framework on which the denial rests. The scoffers appeal to uniformitarianism: 'all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation' (v. 4). The world operates by uniform natural processes; there is no basis for expecting a divine interruption. Peter's counter-attack is historical and theological: the world has already been interrupted — twice — by the word of God (creation from water, and the flood), and the same word that brought those interventions has promised a third. Uniformitarianism has already been falsified by the history the scoffers claim to cite.

Then comes the pastoral heart of the chapter — the motive for the apparent delay. God is not slow. He is patient — long-suffering, holding back His power — because He is 'not willing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' (v. 9). The delay is not absence. It is mercy. Every day before the Day is a day of grace, an open door of repentance. When the Day comes — sudden, certain, like a thief — it will be final. But it will come into a world still being offered the gospel, and that is the point.

The chapter closes with what may be the most ethically charged question in the epistle: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11). Not: When will it happen? The return of Christ is not a date to calculate but a character to cultivate. Holiness, godliness, eagerness for the Day, diligence to be found spotless — this is the life shaped by a hope that is certain. And the letter ends where it began: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity.
3.text: "The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed." (2 Pet. 3:9–10 ESV) "But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells." (2 Pet. 3:13 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Scoffers and the Promise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter has spent chapter 2 describing false teachers and their certain condemnation. Now he turns to their theological weapon — the one argument that does the most damage: the apparent failure of the parousia promise. The Lord said he was coming. He has not come. The first generation has died. Nothing has changed. Therefore the promise was false, and the moral accountability it implied can be safely set aside. This is the logic of the scoffers, and it is formidable — formidable enough that Peter devotes the longest sustained argument in the letter to refuting it.

His counter-move is elegantly historical. The scoffers appeal to uniform continuity: all things continue as they have from the beginning. Peter grants the framework — and then fills it with history. The world has not continued uniformly. It was interrupted twice by the word of God: once in creation (the world formed from water by God's word) and once in judgment (that same world destroyed by water through God's word). The pattern is not continuity; it is creation, interruption, re-creation. The scoffers' own history falsifies their case — and the third interruption, by fire, is reserved and certain by that same word.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wilful Ignorance and the Suppression of Truth

Verse 5 — 'it escapes their notice' — uses a word that implies deliberate willingness to be ignorant. Peter is not describing honest intellectual error; he is describing the wilful suppression of truth (cf. Romans 1:18 — 'they suppress the truth in unrighteousness'). The scoffers know the history; they choose to overlook it because it is inconvenient to their argument. Reformed apologetics has always insisted that unbelief is never merely intellectual — it is moral. The problem is not insufficient evidence but unwillingness to receive what the evidence implies. Every generation of Christian witness faces this: the argument that 'nothing has changed' is always available, always feels sophisticated, and is always in the service of the desire to escape moral accountability.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The death of the first generation was the scoffers' primary exhibit. The apostles had promised that the Lord would return — and the apostles themselves were now dying, and he had not. Peter's two historical counter-examples (creation and flood) were drawn from texts the scoffers themselves would have known — Genesis and the Flood narrative were not in dispute. The argument is not: trust our promise. It is: look at your own history. The word that made the world and destroyed it has spoken again, and it will not return void.

Now: The twenty-first century scoffer's argument is more sophisticated but structurally identical. Two thousand years of non-arrival. Scientific consensus on natural uniformity. The same logic, the same moral motive. Peter's response is the same: the word of God has already done what uniformitarianism says it cannot do — twice. The third act is not less certain for being long-awaited.

verseByVerse.quote: Scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Scoffers' (v. 3) — the same word appears in Jude 18, a shared apostolic tradition about end-time false teachers. These are not intellectual skeptics raising honest questions but people whose theology serves their lifestyle: walking according to their own desires. The argument is post hoc rationalisation. They want to be free of moral constraint, and the elimination of the parousia provides philosophical cover for the freedom they have already chosen.

'Where is the promise of his coming?' (v. 4) — the challenge is sophisticated. The scoffers note that the first generation has died and nothing has changed: all things continue as from the beginning of creation. This is proto-uniformitarianism: nature operates by consistent laws that admit of no divine interruption. The apostolic promise of the parousia has been falsified by the uniformity of historical experience.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'It escapes their notice' — deliberately (v. 5). The ignorance is wilful: they are willing to be ignorant. This is the most important epistemological observation in the chapter. The scoffers are not examining the evidence neutrally and reaching honest conclusions. They have decided what they want to believe, and they are ignoring what contradicts it. The suppression of truth (cf. Rom. 1:18) is always wilful, never merely intellectual.

Peter's counter-argument is elegant. The uniformitarians appeal to history, so Peter goes to history — and finds two catastrophic exceptions to uniformity already on record. First: creation itself. The world was formed out of water and through water, by the word of God. The word made the world; it can unmake and remake it. Second: the flood. The same world formed by God's word was destroyed by it (v. 6). Uniformity had already been interrupted twice. The third intervention — fire — is equally certain: they are 'stored up for fire' (v. 7). The same word that created, flooded, and reserved — will ignite.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Lord's Patience and the Coming Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having demolished the philosophical case for uniformitarianism, Peter now addresses the pastoral question behind it: why hasn't the Day come? The answer is not apologetic but doxological — and it is one of the most beautiful things in the New Testament. God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not the patience of the absent or indifferent; it is the patience of the One who is not willing that any should perish, who is holding back the Day so that the door of repentance remains open. Every sunrise is an act of mercy. Every day before the Day is a day of grace.

Then, with equal force, comes the certainty: the Day of the Lord will come like a thief — suddenly, finally, irreversibly. The heavens will pass away, the elements will dissolve, the earth and its works will be exposed. The fire is not punitive only; it is revelatory — it strips away every concealment and lays bare what is true. And beyond the fire: a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The dissolution is not annihilation; it is purification. Peter closes his eschatological argument not with catastrophe but with promise: the world God made very good will be made, by grace and fire, even better.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Patience and the Will of God in Salvation

Second Peter 3:9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' The 'you' and 'any' must be read in context: Peter addresses the elect community ('toward you'). Reformed theology reads the 'all' as the full complement of the elect — all who will come to repentance within the span of God's patience. This is not universalism; the Day will still close the door. And it is not a contradiction of election; God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered before the end. It is the breathtaking truth that every day of apparent delay is a day of active divine love — the Judge exercising his patience because he is also the Saviour, and he is not finished saving.

On the new creation (v. 13): Herman Bavinck's axiom — 'grace restores nature' — finds its ultimate expression here. The fire of v. 10 does not destroy creation but purifies it; the new heavens and new earth are this creation glorified. The word for 'new' (kainos) means new in quality, not new as in replacement. Christian hope is therefore not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Christians who first received this letter were living in the overlap of promise and apparent delay — as every generation of believers has done. The pressure to conclude that the promise was empty was real. Peter's answer is not more evidence for a near return; it is a reframing of the apparent delay as mercy. The non-arrival of the Day is the patience of the Saviour who is still gathering those who are his.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the pastoral question that follows from the theology. The return is certain; the timing is unknown; the character of the waiting person is therefore everything. The Christian who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live with moral seriousness, gospel urgency, and an eagerness for righteousness that the world cannot understand. The eschatology shapes the ethics — and if the ethics are soft, the eschatology has not yet done its work.

verseByVerse.quote: With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day' (v. 8, citing Ps. 90:4). This is not a prophetic formula for calculating timelines. It is a statement about God's relationship to time: He is not bound by the sequence of moments as creatures are. What feels like slowness from inside time looks different from eternity. The scoffers measure God's faithfulness by their own impatience and find Him wanting — but their clock is the wrong instrument for measuring the One who inhabits eternity.

'He is patient toward you' (v. 9). This patience is not passivity but active restraint of power in the service of a purpose — the restraint of power in the service of a purpose. And the purpose is breathtaking: He is 'not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.' Every day before the Day is a day of open grace, a day in which the door of repentance has not yet been shut. The delay is not God's weakness. It is His mercy — the mercy that led Paul to the same conclusion: 'the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience' are meant to lead to repentance (Rom. 2:4). The Judge is also the Saviour, and He is not finished saving.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar… But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The Day of the Lord will come like a thief' (v. 10). The image (cf. Matt. 24:43; 1 Thess. 5:2; Rev. 3:3; 16:15) emphasises not surprise but suddenness and irreversibility. When a thief has come, there is no undoing it. The Day arrives once and finally, with no opportunity for last-minute preparation. The heavens will pass away with a roar — the onomatopoeic word suggesting the rushing, crackling sound of fire consuming. The stoicheia — elements, heavenly bodies, or the elemental structures of the cosmos — will be dissolved and the earth and its works exposed, laid bare, found out. There is no hiding on that Day.

But the fire is not the final word. We are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, according to His promise (v. 13). The word for 'new' means new in quality, renewed — not merely a replacement. The dissolution is not annihilation but purification — the burning away of all that corrupts, the refinement of creation into its glorified form. And the defining characteristic of the new heavens and new earth is Righteousness dwells there — not righteousness visiting, not righteousness tolerated, but righteousness as the permanent resident and atmosphere of the new creation. This is Isaiah 65:17 and Revelation 21:1 heard together: the world God always intended, finally arrived.

Textual variant — ‘exposed’ or ‘burned up’? (v. 10): The final clause of v. 10 is one of the most contested in the NT text. The ESV follows the best-attested Greek reading: heurethēsetai<\/em> — ‘will be found’ or ‘will be exposed.’ Other manuscripts read katakaēsetai<\/em> — ‘will be burned up.’ The difference matters. If ‘burned up,’ the earth is annihilated. If ‘exposed\/found,’ the fire is revelatory — it strips away all concealment and lays the works of the earth bare before God’s judgment. The ‘exposed’ reading, being the more difficult (scribes would naturally smooth it to ‘burned up’), is almost certainly original — and it supports the renewal rather than annihilation reading of v. 13. The fire purifies and reveals; what survives is what is genuine. This connects directly to 1 Corinthians 3:13–15, where the fire of the Day tests each person’s work — some survives, some is burned away. The new creation of v. 13 is therefore not a replacement universe built from nothing after the old is annihilated; it is this creation refined, purified, and glorified — the world revealed as it truly is when everything false has been burned away. Bavinck: grace restores nature. The fire is the ultimate proof of that restoration.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Final Words: Diligence, Paul, and Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter's final movement draws together eschatology and ethics, apostolic authority and doxology. 'Therefore' — because the Day is coming, because the new creation is promised, because God is patient and will not always be: be diligent. The waiting is not passive. The certain hope is an active shaper of present character — pressing toward the Day with a life that will be found 'without spot or blemish and at peace' when the Searcher arrives.

The remarkable aside in vv. 15–16 is Peter reaching across the church to commend Paul. Their names together — Peter and Paul, rock and apostle to the Gentiles, once publicly at odds over the table fellowship (Gal. 2:11) — now appear together as joint witnesses to the same eschatological patience of God. More remarkably, Peter explicitly calls Paul's letters 'Scripture' — placing them alongside the other Scriptures as the word of God. The canon is not a late construction; it is being attested here, at the close of the apostolic age, by an eyewitness. The letter ends where it began: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ — and to him be the glory, now and to the day of eternity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Canon of Scripture and the Witness of Peter

Verse 16's placement of Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures' (tas loipas graphas) is one of the most important canonical statements in the New Testament. Peter does not say Paul writes wisely or helpfully — he says Paul writes Scripture. The same Greek word used throughout the NT for the inspired writings of the Old Testament is applied here to Paul's letters while the ink was barely dry on them. This destroys the argument that the canon is a fourth-century ecclesiastical construction: the apostles themselves recognized the canonical weight of each other's writing. The church's later formal recognition of the canon did not create it — it acknowledged what the Spirit had already confirmed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people who twisted Paul's letters (v. 16) — 'the ignorant and unstable' — were presumably within the communities that received this letter. The problem was not that they rejected Paul; it was that they used him selectively, wresting the passages on grace and freedom from their ethical context to support the licentiousness Peter has been condemning throughout the letter. The antidote is the same then as now: read Paul in full, read him as Scripture (which means read him expecting to be addressed, not merely informed), and submit to what the whole of his teaching requires.

Now: The letter's final command — 'grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ' — is simultaneously the simplest and the most demanding instruction in the epistle. It means there is no arrival point in this life. There is only growth — deeper grace received, fuller knowledge gained, a Person known more truly, a character conformed more consistently. The false teachers promised a shortcut; Peter offers a lifetime. The doxology that follows it is the ground that makes the command possible: to him be the glory. The one who is worthy of all glory is the one whose grace sustains the growing, whose knowledge is the destination of the journey, and whose day is the horizon toward which all Christian life is oriented.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these things, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace… just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Therefore, beloved… be diligent' (v. 14). This is the ethical conclusion to the eschatological argument. The return of Christ is not primarily a date to calculate but a character to cultivate. The waiting person is not passive — they are diligent, straining toward the moment they know is coming, shaping their present by the future that is certain. To be found by Him 'without spot or blemish and at peace.' The Day comes as an evaluation — not of justification (that is settled in Christ) but of the life lived from it. The believer who has received the divine nature (1:4) and added virtue to faith (1:5–7) will be found as they truly are.

Verses 15–16 contain one of the most remarkable statements in the New Testament. Peter commends Paul's letters — specifically naming them — and then describes the ignorant and unstable who twist them 'as they do the other Scriptures' (v. 16). Paul's letters are placed alongside the other Scriptures. This is a canonical claim of the highest order: Peter, writing at the end of his life, with apostolic authority, acknowledges Paul's letters as Scripture. The NT canon is not a fourth-century invention; its core is attested here, by an eyewitness, before the close of the apostolic age.

verseByVerse.quote: But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ' (v. 18). The letter began with grace and peace multiplied through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord (1:2). It ends with the same coordinates: grace and knowledge. The circularity is deliberate — this is the whole Christian life. Not a list of achievements, not a hierarchy of spiritual states, not a programme of self-improvement. It is a relationship deepened, a Person known more truly, a grace received more fully. The false teachers offered secret knowledge and libertine freedom; Peter offers the knowledge that is grace and the freedom that is holiness.

To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. The doxology is the letter's final word and its deepest word. To whom belongs the glory? Not to the scoffers, who will be silenced by the Day they denied. Not to the false teachers, whose condemnation has not been idle (2:3). Not to human wisdom or philosophical sophistication. To Him — the Lord and Saviour, the One coming, the One patient, the One who does not wish any to perish — to Him be the glory. Now, in the present age of waiting and grace. And to the day of eternity — that day toward which all other days are moving, when patience will become presence, promise will become sight, and the new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells will be home forever. Amen.

3.theology:
Uniformitarianism and the Word of God: Peter's refutation of the scoffers in vv. 5–7 is a model of theological apologetics. The uniformitarians claim that the world operates by consistent natural processes. Peter grants the observation and then shows that the historical record — the record the uniformitarians themselves appeal to — contains two catastrophic interruptions of the very uniformity they invoke: creation and the flood. Both were brought about by the word of God. The same word that did those things has spoken again, and the third act — the fire — is as certain as the first two. The apologist who begins with Scripture's own historical witness is standing on solid ground.

Divine patience and the will of God in salvation: Verse 9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' Reformed theology reads this in its literary context: 'toward you' — the elect community. The 'all' is the full complement of those for whom God's patience is being exercised — all who will come to repentance within the span of His patience. This is not universalism (the Day will still come and shut the door), and it is not a contradiction of election (God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered). It is the breathtaking truth that the apparent delay of the parousia is not divine procrastination — it is divine love, actively gathering those who are His.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 is the eschatological horizon of the entire epistle — and of the entire New Testament. Herman Bavinck's axiom — grace restores nature — finds its ultimate expression here: the fire does not destroy the creation but purifies it; the new creation is this creation glorified, the world God made very good and will make even better. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future demonstrates that the new earth is not a replacement but a renewal — which is why Christian hope is not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and serve and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.

Then: The scoffers' question — 'Where is the promise of his coming?' — has been asked in every generation. The first generation of believers died; the second, the third, the hundredth. Each generation has faced the apparent delay, and the temptation to conclude that the promise was empty. Peter's answer remains the same across every generation: God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not weakness — it is mercy in motion, gathering those who are still to be gathered before the door closes. Every generation of Christians lives in the overlap of promise and fulfilment, patience and urgency.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the most searching pastoral question the letter asks, and it lands as heavily today as it did in the first century. The return of Christ has not yet come — but it is coming, and it is certain. The question is not about calculation but about formation. The person who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, with detachment from the world's false securities, with eager longing for righteousness. The Christian who has domesticated eschatology into a theological opinion without ethical bite has not yet let 2 Peter 3 do its work. Let it. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. That is the whole assignment — and it will last exactly until the Day of eternity.
